about: A string literal holds the text its escapes denote, on every engine: the lexer reads each literal once into that text and every backend writes the text through its own string-literal escaper. Each event assigns `held` a literal whose spelling, pasted between double quotes, would break a target's literal or change its meaning: a quote of either kind, a backslash, a Kotlin template expression, a Swift interpolation, a line break and a tab, `\x` and `\u` escapes, a character past the Basic Multilingual Plane as a braced code point and as a surrogate pair, and a pair of question marks C reads as the start of a trigraph. `measure` reads the UTF-8 bytes of the text, not of its spelling. Expected values are derived from ECMA-262's reading of each literal, not observed from a backend.

steps.note: a double quote inside a single-quoted literal is a double quote
a single quote inside a double-quoted literal is a single quote
an escaped backslash is one backslash
a dollar sign opens no template expression: the text is the ten characters written
a backslash before a parenthesis opens no interpolation
`\n` and `\t` are a line break and a tab
`\x41`, `\u00e9` and `\u{20ac}` are an `A`, an `e` with an acute accent and a euro sign
one, two and three bytes: six, though the spelling is eighteen characters
a braced code point and a surrogate pair both name U+10348
U+10348 is four bytes, so two of them are eight
two question marks and an equals sign are three characters, not a C trigraph
